title: How to Make Testing More Sustainable
author: Ben Linders
gist: Jochen Joswig (via a Ben Linders interview/writeup) argues sustainable ('green') software testing — fail-fast test ordering, change-scoped test execution, per-test energy tracking, and static analysis tools like Creedengo — cuts both compute cost and emissions, and predicts rising energy costs plus EU regulation will push efficiency from a nice-to-have to a competitive advantage.

insights.claim: Jochen Joswig argues a sustainable testing strategy starts by eliminating unnecessary tests and test cases, which both reduces testing time and satisfies minimalism/efficiency criteria for the pipeline.
insights.speaker: Jochen Joswig
insights.so_what: A concrete, low-cost cost/energy optimization lever (test suite pruning) that engineering orgs can apply immediately to cut CI compute spend, independent of any sustainability mandate.
insights.quote: By using a sustainable testing strategy, you can skip unnecessary tests, ensure failing fast and early, and only run tests affected by code changes, Jochen Joswig suggested

insights.claim: Joswig recommends designing test execution so that once a test fails, remaining tests are halted, since unit tests typically run first and catching an error there means integration, end-to-end, and UI tests never need to run, saving energy and time.
insights.speaker: Jochen Joswig
insights.so_what: Fail-fast CI pipeline design is a direct, quantifiable lever on cloud compute cost for any org running large test suites — a practical DevOps efficiency pattern with immediate ROI.
insights.quote: By designing the testing strategy, so that tests fail fast and early, because once a test fails, the execution of the rest can be halted, thus saving energy and time.

insights.claim: Joswig recommends running only tests affected by a code change (especially in monorepos — e.g., skip backend tests when only frontend changed), and going further by running static code analysis first to determine which tests are actually affected.
insights.speaker: Jochen Joswig
insights.so_what: Change-scoped test selection is a well-known CI optimization technique; framing it explicitly as an emissions/energy lever gives it a new business justification (ESG/regulatory) beyond pure speed, which could accelerate tooling adoption in this space.
insights.quote: He suggested executing only tests that test the code that has changed. This is particularly true for all automated tests in monorepo projects.

themes.theme: Measuring and tooling for energy efficiency

insights.claim: Joswig suggests tracking energy consumption of each individual test during execution, feeding it into observability stacks, and raising alarms when methods or runs exceed energy thresholds to incentivize re-engineering inefficient code; where direct energy data isn't available, proxy metrics like MB transferred, time, CPU, and memory utilization can substitute.
insights.speaker: Jochen Joswig
insights.so_what: Points to an emerging tooling niche — per-test energy/carbon observability — that could become a checkbox feature in CI/observability platforms (Datadog-adjacent vendors) as sustainability reporting requirements grow.
insights.quote: you can try to track energy consumption of each individual test during execution and feed that into your observability stack, raising alarms if certain methods or runs exceed energy thresholds

insights.claim: Joswig recommends static code analysis to catch easy-to-spot inefficiencies (e.g., backend calls or database queries inside a loop), naming Creedengo — an open-source SonarQube plugin supporting Java, Python, JavaScript, and C# — as a tool, while noting unverified closed-source pay-to-use alternatives may offer broader language support.
insights.speaker: Jochen Joswig
insights.so_what: Names a specific open-source tool (Creedengo) gaining traction in the green-software-engineering space, worth watching as a bellwether for SonarQube-ecosystem plugin adoption and for competing commercial code-efficiency scanners.
insights.quote: There is Creedengo, an open-source plugin for SonarQube. It supports Java, and also other languages like Python, JavaScript, and C#.
insights.locator: para on static code analysis tools

insights.claim: Creedengo's rule set has a caveat: some rules have negligible real impact on performance and energy consumption, so Joswig advises hand-picking a useful subset rather than applying the full rule set.
insights.speaker: Jochen Joswig
insights.so_what: A practical caution against treating green-coding lint rules as uniformly valuable — teams should validate rule-level impact before wholesale adoption, avoiding false confidence in tooling-driven sustainability claims.
insights.quote: Some of its rules have a negligible impact on performance and energy consumption. Therefore, it is important to hand-pick a useful subset of rules

themes.theme: The greenest code is the code you never write

insights.claim: Joswig stresses testing early with low-fidelity click-dummies or paper prototypes so teams focus development effort only on features that actually add value to users, framed under the motto 'the greenest code is the code you never write.'
insights.speaker: Jochen Joswig
insights.so_what: Reframes lean/agile prototyping practices (already common for cost reasons) as a sustainability argument too — a rhetorical convergence that could help sell agile/lean adoption in orgs newly motivated by ESG mandates.
insights.quote: the greenest code is the code you never write

insights.claim: Joswig argues sustainable/green software development is a team-wide effort extending even to the product owner — e.g., specifying that older/weaker hardware must remain supported and instructing the team to test on such devices for compatibility, which extends hardware lifespan and reduces emissions and waste from hardware replacement.
insights.speaker: Jochen Joswig
insights.so_what: Extending device support windows is a demand-side lever against e-waste and hardware refresh cycles, relevant to hardware OEMs' replacement-cycle economics if broadly adopted as a software design norm.
insights.quote: The resulting extended lifespan of the hardware reduces emissions and harmful effects associated with replacing said hardware.

themes.theme: Instrumentation as a side benefit: security discovery

insights.claim: Andres Freund discovered the CVE-2024-3094 vulnerability (a critical, widely publicized backdoor) almost as a byproduct of performance-oriented testing/investigation, illustrating that deep instrumentation of software behavior can surface critical security issues incidentally.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: A real-world precedent that investing in fine-grained software observability (originally for performance/energy reasons) has a secondary payoff of catching supply-chain-level security vulnerabilities — a case for higher observability investment beyond pure sustainability ROI.
insights.quote: A similar approach has led to the vital discovery of a critical vulnerability, which is now listed in the NIST national vulnerability database under CVE-2024-3094.

themes.theme: Forward-looking predictions: cost, competitive advantage, regulation

insights.claim: Joswig predicts electricity demand for software development will increase in the coming years, which could raise costs and make energy/hardware cost a factor determining the profitability of innovations, with increasing efficiency becoming a competitive advantage.
insights.speaker: Jochen Joswig
insights.so_what: A direct macro linkage: rising compute/energy costs (plausibly AI-driven) will make software efficiency a P&L-relevant competitive differentiator, not just an ESG talking point — relevant to how investors should value engineering-efficiency tooling and green-software startups.
insights.quote: I expect the electricity demand for software development to increase in the next few years. This increase in demand could lead to an increase in cost; hence, the cost of energy and hardware will remain a factor and will determine the profitability of innovations.
insights.locator: interview answer on future of sustainable software development

insights.claim: Joswig expects the free market to be slow to adopt green software best practices, while governments — especially in the EU — already have IT sustainability on their radar, predicting government contracts and tenders will increasingly include IT sustainability requirements, potentially cascading adoption through supply chains.
insights.speaker: Jochen Joswig
insights.so_what: A specific regulatory-driven adoption thesis: EU procurement rules could become a forcing function for green-software compliance tooling and vendor certification, ahead of private-sector voluntary adoption — worth tracking EU tender language for IT sustainability clauses as a leading indicator.
insights.quote: Governments, especially in the EU, have IT sustainability already on their radar, and I expect contracts and tenders issued by governmental organs to include points on IT sustainability and sustainable software, hopefully creating a cascade of adoption throughout the supply chain.
